lead: Hydrographic surveying measures depth and position in water bodies. Underground surveying carries surface coordinates and direction below ground. Both extend control beyond dry land: one through water, one down a shaft. An echo sounder turns two-way sound travel time into depth. Tide reduction converts that depth to chart datum. GNSS or a total station fixes each sounding. Underground, a shaft transfers coordinates and azimuth to a tunnel traverse. Only a few universities teach this as a full topic. Ports, dredging, dams and metro tunnels use it.
prereq: You need 5.1 total station, 5.2 GNSS and Unit 3 levelling for heights and control.

blocks.text: An echo sounder has a transducer under the boat. It sends a short sound pulse down and receives the echo from the bed. The timer records the two-way travel time t. The pulse goes down and back, so one-way path is half the total. A transducer converts electrical energy to sound and back. The bed gives a strong echo.

blocks.where: d is depth below the transducer in metres, c is sound speed in the water in m/s, and t is the two-way travel time in seconds. In sea water c is about 1500 m/s. It varies with temperature, salinity and pressure, so use a measured value.

items: Fix the boat position at every sounding.
Record depth, position and tide height.

blocks.text: This is the same travel-time idea as 5.4 LiDAR, with sound in water instead of light in air. Sounding lines are spaced so the bed is covered.

Bathymetry is water depth measurement. Depth needs a position. A sounding plan sets parallel runs across the area and cross lines to check coverage. GNSS fixes the boat; a total station fixes near-shore marks. Each sounding is stored as a triple: position, depth, time. The sounding plan spacing depends on map scale and the least depth expected.

Chart datum is a low-water reference, close to lowest astronomical tide. A chart shows depth below datum, not below the moving surface. Tide height h is water level above chart datum at sounding time. Reduced depth D = d + h. If the tide is below chart datum, h is negative. A tide gauge or predicted tide gives h.

A bathymetric chart plots reduced depth at position, with shoreline and symbols. Depth contours join equal reduced depths. Cross lines expose gaps and position errors. Dredging, navigation and reservoir capacity use the chart. The chart is final.

Underground survey begins at surface control. GNSS or a total station gives coordinates and height at the shaft collar. Two plumb wires or a laser transfer a vertical line down the shaft. A gyrotheodolite, or the two wires, gives azimuth: the horizontal angle of a line from north. Check the transfer before extending the traverse.

An underground traverse starts at the shaft station. A total station measures angles and distances along the tunnel and carries coordinates to the face. The surveyor sets out the centreline and grade, the designed slope. Two headings meet at breakthrough; breakthrough error is the difference between the faces. Azimuth transfer error grows with distance, so check with cross headings.

Levels transfer by tape or laser; check against a surface benchmark. Traverse adjustment uses the same closing error ideas as Unit 2. Mine and tunnel work call this mine surveying or underground surveying. The surface benchmark controls tunnel level.

figure.caption: Surface control fixes the boat or shaft. The echo sounder gives two-way time, tide reduction gives chart depth, and the shaft carries coordinates and azimuth underground.

spec.title: Depth and underground survey flow
spec.aria: Two linked flows: surface control to echo sounder, tide reduction, and chart; surface control to shaft transfer and underground traverse.

examples.question: An echo sounder records a two-way travel time of 0.040 s. Sound speed in water is 1500 m/s. The tide is 1.20 m above chart datum. Find the depth below the water surface and the reduced depth below chart datum.
steps: Depth d = c × one-way time = 1500 × 0.020 = 30.0 m.
Reduced depth D = d + h = 30.0 + 1.20 = 31.2 m.
The tide is positive because it is above chart datum.
examples.answer: Depth below the water surface is 30.0 m; reduced depth below chart datum is 31.2 m.
examples.check:
c = 1500.0
t = 0.040
h = 1.20
d = c * t / 2
D = d + h
print(d)
print(D)

traps: Using t instead of t/2 gives double the depth.
Subtracting the tide when it is above chart datum; D = d + h.
Mixing sound speed units, for example 1500 m/s with t in milliseconds.
Calling chart datum the sea surface; it is a fixed low-water reference.

quiz.q: What does an echo sounder measure directly?
Why is travel time divided by 2?
quiz.a: The pulse travels down and back; one-way path is half.

quiz.q: A sounder gives t = 0.060 s and c = 1500 m/s. Find depth.
Tide is −0.30 m relative to chart datum and d = 12.0 m. Find reduced depth.
quiz.a: D = 12.0 + (−0.30) = 11.7 m; negative tide reduces chart depth.

quiz.q: Why transfer azimuth down a shaft?
quiz.a: To start the traverse in the surface reference direction.

quiz.q: Name two causes of tunnel breakthrough error.
quiz.a: Azimuth transfer error and traverse angle or distance error; shaft coordinate and level errors also count.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern hydrographic work uses multibeam echo sounders, side-scan sonar and inertial navigation to map many depths per second. Tunnel guidance uses gyrotheodolites, lasers and total stations linked to tunnel boring machines. Search terms: multibeam bathymetry, sound velocity profile, gyro orientation, tunnel breakthrough survey.
